issues.legal_issue: A conviction for rioting may be sustained even when fewer than five persons are identified or convicted, if the evidence establishes that the accused belonged to an unlawful assembly of at least five persons.
material_facts: Fourteen persons were charged with rioting, but the other thirteen were acquitted because they were not properly identified as participants.
The courts found that the appellant was in the mob and that the assembly comprised at least five persons, whether identified or not.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal of the other thirteen did not prevent the appellant from being convicted of rioting, because the evidence supported a finding that he was a member of an assembly of five or more persons.
issues.legal_principle: Section 141 of the Indian Penal Code defines an unlawful assembly, and section 147 applies where a person commits rioting as a member of such an assembly. The identity of every member is distinct from the question whether the assembly had at least five members; the latter may be established even if fewer than five are identified or convicted.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_rioting_case: The proceeding concerns a person's conviction for rioting as a member of an alleged unlawful assembly.
predicates.fewer_than_five_members_identified_or_co: Fewer than five alleged members of the assembly are identified or convicted.
predicates.evidence_establishes_assembly_of_five_or: The evidence establishes that the accused belonged to an assembly containing at least five people, whether identified or unidentified.

issues.definition: When a rioting case concerns an assembly shown to have at least five members, the accused's conviction may be sustained even if fewer than five members are identified or convicted.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing an appeal from a rioting conviction must make a definite finding on possession when the charged common object includes dispossessing a person and possession is material to determining the assembly's object, the aggressor, or the availability of private defence.
material_facts: The charge alleged that the assembly's common object included dispossessing the complainant from disputed land, as well as assaulting and murdering others.
The trial court found that possession of the land was disputed but made no determination of who possessed it at the time of the occurrence.

The High Court treated possession as immaterial and upheld the rioting conviction, although the possession issue could affect whether the accused's party was dispossessing the complainant and whether private defence was available.
The Supreme Court considered the absence of a definite finding on possession a serious defect and remanded the appeal for rehearing.
issues.conclusion: The conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appeal was remanded to the High Court for rehearing and a definite finding on possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 141 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code, the alleged common object is material to whether an assembly is unlawful and whether its members committed rioting. Where the prosecution frames dispossession as a central common object, possession cannot be dismissed as immaterial if it bears on that object, on who was the aggressor, or on private defence. Failure to determine that vital issue may cause serious and substantial injustice warranting appellate intervention.

predicates.charged_common_object_includes_disposses: The charge alleges that the assembly's common object included dispossessing a person from land.

issues.definition: If a rioting appeal involves a disputed possession issue central to the charged object or defence and the appellate court leaves that issue unresolved, the conviction and sentence are set aside and the appeal is remanded for a finding.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere in a criminal matter on special leave when a violation of fundamental principles of justice or a grave and substantial miscarriage of justice has occurred, but not merely because of an error that caused no such injustice.
material_facts: The matter was a criminal appeal admitted by special leave.
The appellate court had left undecided a vital possession issue that affected assessment of the alleged common object and who was the aggressor.
The Supreme Court found that this omission was capable of causing serious and substantial injustice and interfered on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The Court applied the established limits on interference in criminal cases and held that the failure to decide the vital possession issue justified its intervention.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it was not bound by Privy Council practice and precedents but saw no reason to depart from their principles governing criminal appeals. It relied on Riel v. The Queen; In re Abraham Mallory Dillet; Ibrahim v. The King; Dal Singh v. King Emperor; Ex Parte Macrea; Taba Singh v. King Emperor; Easwaramurthi v. Emperor; George G. Feller v. The King; Md. Afdal Khan v. Abdul Hahman; and Louis Edouard Lanier v. The King. Those authorities establish that special-leave interference requires a clear departure from justice, a violation of natural justice, or serious and substantial injustice; an error or irregularity alone is insufficient where it has not caused a grave miscarriage of justice.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.serious_substantial_injustice: A failure by a lower court to decide a material issue causes or threatens grave and substantial injustice to the accused.
predicates.fundamental_fairness_violation: The proceedings violate fundamental principles of natural justice or deprive the accused of the substance of a fair trial and the protection of the law.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal brought by special leave, the Supreme Court may interfere when serious and substantial injustice or a fundamental fairness violation is present.
